questions.text:
Te Kanikani ā-Kura — te wāhanga tuatahi / The school dance — part one

Read the text about Hana and her friends preparing for the school dance. The passage describes how Whaea Mere, their kaiako, organised a school disco but faced a problem finding a suitable venue because the school hall was being repaired. The whānau room was too small for all the students. Whaea Mere eventually persuaded the principal to allow use of the gymnasium.

Kuputaka: wāhi = place/venue; nāwai rā = after a time; whakamana = to agree/approve

Whakamāramatia mai te raru o te kura me te rautaki hei whakaea.
Explain the school's problem and how it was resolved.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Identifies that they have no venue for the school dance.
- States that Whaea Mere got permission to use the gymnasium.
- May include that the hall was being repaired.
- May include basic errors in details or interpretation.

For Merit:
- Explains that they cannot use the school hall because it is being repaired.
- Notes that the whānau room is too small for all the students.
- Explains that Whaea Mere persuaded the principal to allow use of the gymnasium.
- Links examples with simple justifications to form a basic argument.

For Excellence:
- Provides a detailed explanation covering three aspects of the venue problem: (1) the school hall was being repaired and could not be used.
- (2) the whānau room was considered but was too small for the number of students wanting to attend.
- (3) the gymnasium was not usually available for social events.
- Explains how Whaea Mere spoke to the principal and convinced her by explaining the importance of the event for student wellbeing.
- Provides a persuasive, well-justified argument with examples that convinces the reader and shows comprehensive understanding of the finer details of the text.

questions.text:
Te Kanikani ā-Kura — te wāhanga tuarua / The school dance — part two

The passage describes Hana's experience getting ready for the dance. She is excited (koa) at first but becomes stressed (āwangawanga) about what to wear. She tries on many outfits but dislikes them all. She borrows a dress from her older sister but feels awkward (whakamā) wearing it. In the end, she chooses her own favourite casual clothes and feels much better.

Kuputaka: koa = happy/joyful; āwangawanga = stressed/worried; whakamā = shy/embarrassed; māia = confident

Whakamāramatia mai ngā whakaaro me ngā kare ā-roto o Hana mō tōna kākahu.
Explain Hana's thoughts and feelings about her outfit.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Identifies that Hana was stressed about her outfit.
- Notes she didn't like the clothes she tried on.

For Merit:
- Explains that Hana was excited about the dance but became stressed when choosing what to wear.
- Notes she tried on many outfits and disliked them all.
- Explains she borrowed her sister's dress but felt awkward/embarrassed wearing it.

For Excellence:
- Provides a comprehensive response: Hana was initially excited about the dance but became increasingly anxious about her outfit.
- She tried on many of her own clothes but felt none of them were right.
- She then borrowed a dress from her older sister but felt whakamā (embarrassed/awkward) because it wasn't her style.
- In the end, she chose her own favourite casual clothes and immediately felt more māia (confident) and comfortable being herself.
- Shows thorough understanding of Hana's emotional journey from excitement through anxiety to self-acceptance.

questions.text:
Te Kanikani ā-Kura — te wāhanga tuatoru / The school dance — part three

The passage describes the evening of the dance. Everyone enjoyed the music and dancing. When it was time to tidy up, some students tried to leave without helping. Hana and her friends stayed behind to help stack chairs, sweep the floor, and collect rubbish. The kaiako was very grateful and the principal said the gymnasium could be used again in future because of how well the students cared for it.

Kuputaka: whakapai = to tidy up; toenga = remainder/leftovers; manaaki = to care for/show hospitality

Whakamāramatia te hāngaitanga o te whakataukī nei, "Mā te huruhuru, ka rere te manu" ki roto i te tuhinga.
Explain how the whakataukī "Mā te huruhuru, ka rere te manu" (It is by feathers that a bird can fly / With help, great things can be achieved) applies to the text.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Identifies a basic connection, e.g.
- they helped tidy up, OR the whakataukī is about helping and contributing.

For Merit:
- Explains that the whakataukī is about everyone contributing to achieve something greater.
- Hana and her friends helped tidy the gymnasium, which meant the principal agreed it could be used again.
- Their individual contributions (stacking chairs, sweeping, collecting rubbish) together achieved the larger goal.

For Excellence:
- Provides a thorough explanation: The whakataukī "Mā te huruhuru, ka rere te manu" is about how individual contributions enable collective success.
- In the context of the text, each student who stayed behind contributed something — Hana stacked chairs, her friends swept and collected rubbish.
- These individual efforts (the feathers) together enabled the 'bird to fly' — the principal was so impressed by how well the students cared for the gymnasium that she agreed it could be used for future events.
- Without each person's contribution, this outcome would not have been achieved.
- Shows understanding of the meaning and purpose of the text and links the whakataukī to specific examples.
